abstract: Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)-based genotyping enables population genomic studies of the history of biological invasions, allowing for inference of source populations and routes of spread. Methods for genotyping include whole genome sequencing (WGS), as well as lower-cost targeted approaches, such as microarrays, hybrid capture, or Genotyping by Sequencing (GBS). Using GBS, we previously genotyped ~2,000 adult zebra mussels collected from over 100 populations across Minnesota, the Great Lakes, and the Upper Mississippi River. The need for sufficient template DNA restricts such genotyping approaches to adult animals, while genotyping lower biomass samples, such as zebra mussel veliger larvae remains challenging. Here, we applied Multiple Displacement Amplification (MDA) to increase DNA concentration from low-biomass samples. We demonstrate that MDA yields reproducible WGS and GBS data from as little as 1 ng of starting material and genotyped single veliger larvae from MDA amplified DNA, accurately assigning them to their known source populations. Furthermore, we showed that inheritance patterns can be tracked in MDA amplified DNA from veliger larvae and demonstrated an approach for forensic genetics of juvenile zebra mussels that were found contaminating "moss balls" and sold in the aquarium pet trade. Pairing MDA with high-resolution genomic workflows overcomes biomass limitations and represents a powerful toolkit to enhance early detection, trace invasion pathways, and mitigate the spread of the invasive zebra mussel. This approach is readily generalizable to other organisms or developmental stages where limiting quantities of DNA are available.
